questions: What does each part of the loop do - the battery, the bulb and the ammeter?
Why does disconnecting one wire switch the whole circuit off?
segments.say: One loop. A circuit is one unbroken loop: battery, bulb, ammeter, wires. The battery pushes charge around the loop, the bulb turns electrical energy into light, and the ammeter measures the flow. Break the loop anywhere and everything stops. Keep your student notes open at the circuit and current definitions for this scene.

questions: Which terminal does conventional current leave, and which does it return to?
How do the red markers show the direction without any words?
segments.say: Direction matters. Conventional current flows out of the battery's positive terminal, around the loop, and back into the negative terminal. Follow the red markers as they crawl along the wires - that crawl is the agreed direction, every time. Check the conventional current definition in your student notes.

questions: Why does one broken bulb switch off a whole series circuit?
Which arrangement keeps the other bulb lit when one fails, and why?
segments.say: One path or many? In series there is only one path, so one broken bulb kills the whole loop. In parallel each bulb sits on its own branch - one can fail and the other stays lit. Decide which arrangement a house should use before we move on. Now try the series-parallel question on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: What changed in this scene - the voltage, the resistance, or both?
What current would a 9 volt battery drive through the same 4 ohm resistor?
segments.say: Ohm's law ties it together: V equals I times R. Watch the dial - the battery steps from 6 to 12 volts, the red markers speed up, and with resistance fixed at 4 ohms the ammeter climbs from 1.5 to 3 amps. Check the arithmetic with the triangle: 12 divided by 4 is 3.

questions: What do the two ammeters read, and where exactly are they placed?
If the bulb does not use up current, what does it use up - or rather, change?
segments.say: Now the trap, head-on. The bulb glows and gets hot, so it feels as though it drinks the current. Put an ammeter anywhere in the series loop - before the bulb, after it - and every meter reads the same 0.5 amps. The bulb changes electrical energy into light and heat; it does not shrink the current. Compare the two readings in your student notes.

questions: Name the three takeaways in your own words.
Which scene proved that current is the same on both sides of the bulb?
segments.say: Electricity in one minute. Three things to carry away: current flows from positive to negative around a single loop; series means one path while parallel means many; and in a series loop the current is identical everywhere, tied together by V equals I R. Then take the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits the used-up claim head-on.
segments.watchFor: The bulb uses up the current. Listen for it in pair talk and watch for it on the exit ticket: The bulb glows and gets hot, so it looks like it consumes the electricity flowing through it. Send them back to the two ammeters and the correct turn: Current is not used up: an ammeter reads the same 0.5 amps on both sides of the bulb.
